Mainlining is a cyberpunk-inspired investigative adventure that turns the ordinary process of browsing files, reading emails, and searching databases into a tense and immersive detective experience. Developed by Rebelephant and published by Merge Games, the game places players behind the screen of a government intelligence computer system where every clue, suspect, and secret must be uncovered through hacking, surveillance, and careful analysis of digital information. Instead of relying on action sequences or cinematic set pieces, Mainlining builds suspense entirely through deduction, atmosphere, and the unsettling realization that every citizen’s private life is only a few clicks away from exposure.

The game is set in a near-future Britain where privacy laws have collapsed following the introduction of the BLU Pill Act, legislation that grants intelligence agencies unrestricted access to personal digital information. Players take on the role of an operative working for MI7, a government surveillance division tasked with tracking cybercriminals after a major breach compromises national security. What initially appears to be a series of disconnected investigations slowly evolves into a larger conspiracy involving corruption, abuse of power, political manipulation, and the dangers of mass surveillance. The story feels particularly effective because its themes mirror real-world debates surrounding government monitoring and digital privacy, giving the experience a level of relevance that extends beyond simple science fiction.

One of Mainlining’s greatest achievements is its presentation. The entire game takes place inside a simulated retro computer operating system inspired by older versions of Windows desktops. Every action occurs through email clients, command prompts, browsers, folders, chat programs, and intelligence databases, creating the illusion that the player is genuinely operating inside a classified surveillance network. This design choice immediately establishes immersion because players interact with the world exactly the way an investigator would. The retro-inspired pixel art and low-tech interface also contribute heavily to the atmosphere, giving the game a gritty and believable cyberpunk identity without relying on flashy visuals.

Gameplay revolves around investigating suspects by hacking into personal computers and analyzing digital traces left behind in their online activity. Players search through conversations, photographs, browsing histories, financial records, and social media interactions in order to uncover evidence and identify criminal behavior. Unlike many detective games that heavily guide the player toward obvious solutions, Mainlining encourages independent thinking and observation. Important clues are often hidden within seemingly unimportant files or casual conversations, forcing players to pay close attention to details instead of simply following objective markers.

The command-line hacking mechanics are surprisingly immersive despite their simplicity. Players use text commands to access networks, trace IP addresses, and infiltrate systems, creating the feeling of performing real investigative work without becoming inaccessible to newcomers. The game succeeds because it understands how to make information itself feel rewarding. Discovering a hidden message, uncovering an encrypted file, or linking multiple suspects together creates genuine excitement because progress depends entirely on the player’s own deductions rather than scripted sequences.

What truly separates Mainlining from other hacking-themed games is the moral discomfort that develops over time. Although the player technically works for law enforcement, many of the investigative methods feel invasive and ethically questionable. Reading intimate personal conversations, examining private photographs, and monitoring every aspect of someone’s digital life creates a constant sense of unease. The game repeatedly raises questions about whether unrestricted surveillance can ever remain justified once governments gain the ability to observe every citizen without limitations. Even when tracking criminals, the player often feels disturbingly close to violating the boundaries of innocent people.

The investigations themselves remain varied enough to keep the campaign engaging. Cases involve cybercrime, hacking groups, drug operations, financial fraud, and organized conspiracies that slowly reveal deeper connections hidden beneath the surface. Players must carefully identify suspects, gather evidence, and determine physical locations before making arrests. Wrong accusations can result in failure, adding pressure to every investigation and encouraging players to double-check conclusions before acting. This structure creates a satisfying detective experience because success feels earned through careful reasoning rather than random guessing.

The writing throughout the game is consistently strong. Dialogue balances serious political themes with dry humor and believable character interactions that prevent the experience from becoming overly bleak. Emails, online chats, and casual conversations reveal small personality details that make suspects and supporting characters feel authentic despite the minimalist presentation. The game gradually builds a believable world where political fear, digital dependence, and government overreach have become deeply intertwined with everyday life.

The soundtrack complements the atmosphere exceptionally well. Electronic music and ambient background tracks create a constant feeling of tension and paranoia without overwhelming the quieter investigative moments. Combined with the glowing retro desktop aesthetic and endless streams of digital information, the audio design reinforces the sense that players are trapped inside a cold and impersonal surveillance system.

Despite its originality, Mainlining is not completely free from flaws. Some investigations can become repetitive because the gameplay loop often revolves around similar patterns of searching files and tracing connections. Certain clues are occasionally too obscure, leading to moments where progression slows due to unclear objectives. The command-line interface, while immersive, can also feel awkward at times because typing errors or unclear system responses occasionally interrupt the pacing. Players expecting action-heavy hacking gameplay may also find the experience too slow because most of the tension comes from reading, analyzing information, and making logical deductions rather than participating in high-energy sequences.

The visual presentation, while stylish, is intentionally minimalistic and may not appeal to everyone. Those expecting large cinematic environments or highly animated storytelling may initially find the desktop-only structure limiting. However, the simplicity ultimately becomes one of the game’s strengths because it keeps the player fully focused on the investigation itself rather than external distractions.

Although it lacks major production values or complex action mechanics, Mainlining stands out as one of the more memorable indie hacking adventures available. Its investigative gameplay, morally ambiguous storytelling, and immersive interface design create a unique experience that rewards patience, observation, and curiosity. Players interested in conspiracy thrillers, cybercrime investigations, and narrative-driven puzzle games will likely find themselves completely absorbed by its dark digital world.

Mainlining is a satirical dystopian hacking adventure where you are the law... The fictional MI-7 in a future where unlicensed software development carries at 25-year jail sentence. Your job as a MI-7 agent is to hack your way across the map, chase down suspects, hack their machines for evidence, then issue arrest warrants which must include their location (which district) as well as what evidence do you offer as evidence of their crime (obtained legally... or not). 

The game pokes fun at current practices as there are callouts of all the major OSs and their UI quirks. The default, Rainbow OS, is clearly Windows, but you'll also find analog for MacOS, Linux, and even Chrome OS. There are also callouts to the various web browsers, major apps like Dropbox (Skybox here), and even live wallpapers. There's also AirTag, IRC, PGP, and so on. And of course, the good ol' command prompt. 

What's interesting is there's often more than one way to solve a case. Generally, the case just needs ONE arrest, but often, you may find several pieces of evidence that lets you chose who to arrest and what for (what evidence to convict them with). 

Not much replay value, but it is fun while it lasts.

Mainlining is a story-driven hacking-flavoured thriller/adventure game with gameplay closer to a point-and-click adventure than than the "Hollywood" hackers (Uplink, etc).

Set in a slightly dystopian near future, you are an MI7 agent empowered to hack into citizen's computers to prevent cybercrime.  Each chapter presents the player with a new crime to solve by finding IPs, connecting to them, downloading documents, and following the trail until you can apply for an arrest warrant.

Graphics and sound are all serviceable, characters dialogue are charming, and the developers put a lot of time into huge suspect database, variety of interfaces, and multiple solutions to each chapter.

Mainlining is solid game from a small indie team, but does lack polish in a few areas. A number of websites that should exist in the game do not, there are numerous spelling errors and several "Welcome, $USERNAME" type bugs, and the in-game tools have a lot of minor UX issues that can be frustrating.  In particular, the warrant system is somewhat notorious for being too exacting, but the cost of failure is low, so it is tolerable.

Overall definitely worth a playthough if you like the demo.

I liked Mainlining at first, because I like the visual style and it also has a backstory (unlike most other "hacking" games).
I would forgive the bad UX of the command prompt and the incompleteness of the universe (e.g. websites only exist for the time of the missions in which they appear) and some other minor issues.

But the dealbreaker for me is how stupid the missions are. You have to identify perpetrators, collect evidence against them and find their whereabouts. Okay - that COULD be fun. But a huge part of the problem is that - when you get one of the ingredients wrong, you get no useful information on WHICH ingredient was wrong. If the location isn't correct, then why does the newspaper say that the suspect had been "wrongly accused" and "released"? This phrasing indicates that the location was right but the evidence to weak. Okay - so the feedback is misleading and (once you have figured THAT out!) you have to look at the clues and logically deduce the ingredients. Right? That would constitute a PUZZLE-game. That would make sense. That would be fun. But that's not how Mainlining rolls.

Oftentimes you have to submit a piece of evidence that would never hold up in court - even when you have collected much better evidence that isn't accepted. Also you often have evidence against multiple suspects. So you are already guessing between 6 to 30 combinations of these two ingredients. As to the whereabouts: you have access to everybodys addresses, but usually there is a vague hint to a different location in one of the files - and I mean VAGUE. And if there isn't such a hint, you are still always in doubt whether you have overlooked one. AND ON TOP OF THAT there are sometimes twists that require leaps in your reasoning that only make sense in hindsight. Mission 7 in particular was so harebrained that I FURIOUSLY uninstalled the game after reading that insult of a "solution" in a walkthrough.

I'm convinced that Rebelephant wasted to much time on side-gimmicks like the "maps" view, ran out of time in development and could only design a handful of missions, so they deliberately made the solutions illogical to artificially extend the playing-time. Illogical puzzle games aren't fun, they are frustrating. VERY FRUSTRATING. So although I really want to like this game - I can only advise you to STAY AWAY from it!

I truly wanted to recommend this game because it has got so many things nicely done. I played a lot of hacking simulation games and when I realized this isn't exactly one of them (hacking in this is all about typing only a handful console commands) I didn't care much, doing some simple detective work and enjoying it as if a visual novel could also be enough for me. 

Firstly, the game is a little buggy and sometimes crashes, I think it crashed 4 times during my playthrough, so I had to start a case from scratch while almost at the point of moving next one, because game autosaves only at the start of a new case. 

The real annoying problem with this game is the 'evidence' part. It is pretty simple. You download a lot of files, find the real names of the devious anti-government hackers who all have nicknames, then find really incriminating documents about them, then you attempt to arrest them using the very obvious document you have seized... but it doesn't work. The game says, with a newspaper article after your attempted to arrest, that the security service you work for has wrongly accused an innocent person. The document, although even the most incriminating one, blatantly mentioning everything about the hacker, his real name and activities is somehow the wrong document... Instead, it is one of the other documents with containing a lot less information, sometimes even not containing any information related to the case. So after awhile you give up, get extremely bored and simply go from file to file, trying each one of them to arrest the suspect and one of them works because devs decided only one of them should work even though there is not a concrete reason why only that one should work. I finished the game, but it was a througly annoying experience. I don't think I could have finished it if the game didn't have such good writing and story.

There are much better hacking simulation games out there, even if you have played all of them, I still recommend skipping this one because it doesn't award the time you spent on going through all those documents. Really badly designed, I don't what they were thinking.

[b]/STORY and CHARACTERS (6/10)/[/b]

First things first, let's start with the story and characters. You're an agent from the government cyber security agency MI7 that investigates with other MI7 agents a group of hackers called Thorn who breached their servers. Your job is to track down all the members of the group and arrest them for a different crime in order to hide the security breach to the public. Alright, sounds simple enough, but that's because it IS simple, it's not more fleshed out than that. You spend the whole game hunting down an entire hacker group, then find an excuse to arrest them (I'll get back on that later). Even when you detain the big leader, none of what you've done felt satisfying after that.

As for the characters, well you don't have that much of character development from them, except for the "smart girl of the team" agent Sharp, the "bossy boss who takes his job way too seriously" Osvalt, the "I prefer old TTS softwares" agent on the field Cooper, the "flirty secretary who puts winky emojis all over her emails" Ashley, the "hahaha, I'm evil" hacker group leader Mr. Blue. Anyway, you get the point. Each character is only limited to one main characteristic and that's it.

[b]/GAMEPLAY (4/10)/[/b]

Oh boy, the gameplay is the main(lining) reason why I'm not recommending this. Jeez, where do I start? Well, first of all, if you're expecting to feel like a hacker, you're in for a disappointment. All you get is a command-prompt application with two script-kiddie commands: one that gets a website's IP and one that hacks into someone's computer using the said IP. That's right, throughout the whole game you'll spend most of your time typing 'ping', 'iphack', 'ping', 'iphack' while searching a computer's files in a DOS-style file navigation system. The devs claimed that it was on purpose in order to emphasize the narration over actual hacking. I would be fine with that kind of decision, but that doesn't mean you should stick to that repetitive "look at a website, ping, iphack and read files" bulls hit. At least keep an enjoyable gameplay in the background as well. Luckily, you get some other apps (like the google map one) and Operating Systems on the way.

On top of that, the arrest system is really nitpicky about which evidence you use against the person. Each case has around three alternate crimes to choose from to arrest the person you're tracking. However, only 1 evidence per crime is accepted code-wise. In other words, if you choose a proof that totally makes sense but wasn't chosen by the devs, it doesn't count. I ended up spamming the "begin arrest" button with every file I snatched.

As for the OS interfaces, it's a buggy mess, no matter which one is it. You start off with a parody Windows XP, which is pretty nice. You also get parody Ubuntu, parody Mac and parody Windows Vista/7 on the way, which is also great. The pixel art is pretty good, but the Operating Systems look so limited in comparison to the real thing, they don't feel like Operating Systems that anyone would actually use in real life (I know it's just a game, but come on). You can't delete files in your folder (too bad if you accidentally downloaded the same thing twice!) and the notepad doesn't save what you wrote into a text file, which is pretty inconvenient when I constantly need to write down IPs and names (and if you accidentally closed the notepad, too bad!). Also, if you keep windows open in Windows XP, then switch to another OS, open windows in that said OS, then switch back to Windows XP, the windows will start overlapping. I'm not impressed, man. Don't you have a "visible/invisible" property on your images or something in the engine you're using? Oh, and you're gonna love this one: the program is so delayed that if you type something way too fast, some keys will be ignored. Most of the time, you're going to have a lot of "mainlining" ending up like "manliin" because the game couldn't keep track of everything you typed down. This is super annoying when you type an IP, but get an error because the fucking game missed a keystroke and you don't know why it doesn't work since the error message doesn't tell you anything about what went wrong.

There are even reports of people who couldn't advance in some cases because the program forgot to add certain chat messages on the left to let you continue, which is frustrating when you can't even save in the middle of a case and instead start the whole thing over again. Luckily, I didn't encounter those case advancement bugs, but if you can't make a OS interface themed game with basic typing and windows manipulation without being overflowed with bugs, you shouldn't even sell it at 8-10 bucks. Personally, from my experience with this game, I think it should be five dollars at best, or even free.

[b]/CONCLUSION/[/b]

To conclude, I don't recommend this game. It's half-baked, it looks like a prototype game and doesn't have any satisfaction upon playing it whatsoever. The replayability value is somewhat there, but I put the game aside about two or three times before finally finishing it. If you feel like buying a hacking game without caring about anything else, then go for it. Otherwise, I'm giving this game...

Allegedly inspired by real life privacy laws being passed in England, Mainlining is a government hacking game where you play as a member of the mysterious agency MI7, aka the "Lions". It's okay though, you're the lightly comedy kind of oppressive government. You've even got an agent who exists entirely to be a walking Twin Peaks reference. Ha ha.

You're allowed via the "BLU Pill Act" to hack into any PC you want, but you can only arrest people if you can produce evidence towards one of three charges: Selling illegal items (5 years), Theft of data or physical items (10 years), or the most heinous, life-destroying crime of all... Unlicensed Software Development (25 years).

The anti-government activist group THORNS however is working on counter-hacking the hackers. Can you capture them before...

...well, nothing actually really happens, because here's the thing: Mainlining is way less a hacking game and more of a traditional point and click adventure. If there's a way to game over, I didn't find it, and I tried things like arresting random people out of the phone book a half-dozen times just to see if the newspaper articles accusing MI7 of being incompetent losers ever got more fed up. (They did not.)

So in practice the tiers of arrest serve as self-imposed difficulty levels for the most part. Poke around a little, find someone selling drugs, arrest them for 5. Or you can poke further, discover they're being framed and arrest the framer for a data violation. Or you can push further and arrest the guy who wrote the software that made it possible for the framer to do his work.

There's no branching plotlines based on who you arrest, you just kind of bomf along to the next case.

You'll have a great idea about where to look next and ... oops, no, that site mentioned in an email doesn't actually exist. 

I spent a fair amount of time towards the endgame going "Oh. Well that should've worked though?" and that's never something you want people saying about your adventure game. I feel like there was a big scope in mind and they had to cut it down and cut it back for actual release.

Mainlining has a lot of cute ideas about the hacking genre, and it's not a total wash of a game. It's just flawed, and you really really have to know that going in.

- [b]Gameplay:[/b]  Interfacing with the game is fairly straightforward. You're using a simulation of a computer desktop. You cannot edit the text freely, so if you want to make a change to something at the top of the file, you'd have to erase everything and start over. Luckily, you'll find that program is mostly useless.

The lame thing is that, for most cases, you can only turn in one-piece of evidence linking the person to the crime, although there may be several in reality. Also, you have to pick the right location for the person, so even if you have the evidence correct, if you don't choose the right location, it somehow ends up as a False Arrest. It doesn't really make any sense that you could have sufficient evidence, but a person is [i][b]Falsely Accused[/b][/i] because they were in a different location than you originally thought they were (i.e. at work instead of at home.) That's just dumb...

- [b]Plot/Story:[/b]  This is also fairly straightforward and not very awe-inspiring. You're working for a Big Brother goverment agency that was hacked and it's your job to bring down the Cyber Terrorists in fine fashion. The story is mostly told through Emails and Documents you find while hacking systems. It is honestly pretty forgettable, and is not very long.

- [b]Graphics:[/b]  This is a very minimalist retro-style game. The text takes a bit to get used to reading, in its pixelated format. There are no actual graphics options for tuning the look of the game.

- [b]Music:[/b]  The soundtrack is actually decent for this type of game. It's nothing to shake a stick at, but was mostly just chill music to give a spy-ish undertone to the game.

- [b]Overall:[/b]  I give the game a [b]6.5/10[/b]. It's fairly short, and was kind of interesting to play through, but it is an utterly forgettable experience that will leave you wanting to play something similar, but with much better design. What made Mainlining an utterly frustrating experience for me was receiving specific instruction in the game that were not correct. There is one mission in particular where your partner says you must provide a legal document to prove that someone had a name change. I did this and failed the mission.
On top of that (same mission), the suspect lived in one area, but had expressed that he was going to move back home with his parents in an email. When I tried arresting the subject in the area where his parents live, I failed the mission and was met with a message that said attempting to make an arrest in that area failed to produce a suspect. I then tried to make an arrest where the suspect stated he lived. I was met with another message that I failed the mission, but that the area I made the arrest produced the suspect. I thought to myself, okay, I now know this person lives in this area, but I must have the wrong evidence. I then tried evidence after evidence, clicking through documents and trying them out in my arrest attempt with the same suspect in the area where he said he lived. I kept receiving fail messages. I thought, okay, maybe I completely missed a small detail and have the wrong suspect.
I reviewed each document in the mission and determined that either I'm totally missing something or I'm experiencing a serious progress bug. I finally quit the game and go online to find out the answer (,which can be a frustrating thing to have to do for a video game). I find out that I had the correct suspect and had the correct evidence at one point in my many attempts, but the location I was attempting the arrest in was incorrect and the suspect was actually in the area where his parents live.
I was incredibly frustrated with this given that the game not only was telling me in my failed attempts that searching for the suspect in the area where his parents live fails to produce a suspect, but also that the 'correct' evidence to produce was not what your AI partner told you to provide and was not even in the top 3 pieces of evidence that seemed like the logical choice. You work for an NSA-type agency called MI7, and spend much of the game learning about a hacker collective called Thorn. Although the game may be attempting to make a statement about government overreach, I'm not sure it really "landed" for me.

Either way, I enjoyed almost the entirety of my time with the game. My main gripes included:

1) The arrest guidelines should always be accessible. They are accessible on the first case, but then you just sort of have to remember them moving forward. A user has published them in a game "guide" through Steam, but they're worth printing out or writing down. You're looking for certain types of crimes, and you'll likely want to arrest individuals for breaking laws that carry the harshest penalty. For instance, you don't want to arrest a suspect for jaywalking when he or she is a probable murderer.

2) The location aspect. Although it makes sense that you need to know where a suspect is for a cop to travel there and arrest them, the location aspect always seemed strange to me. It was either so obvious that it was pointless to point out, or it was bizarrely hidden. One one case I had to consult a guide to find the correct location - apparently it was in a picture that I found, seen through paying attention to buildings in the background?

3) As other reviews have noted, there are some UI issues. Sometimes the game would "lock" you in a certain window, meaning that no matter what window you were currently working in, text would only transmit to a certain one. The only fix I found here was to close all windows other than the one you wanted your text to appear in. However, this could be frustrating. The game has a notepad, which is actually very useful, because there are always server IPs and passwords you wanted to write down, and this way you don't have to cover your actual desktop in notes. However, closing the notepad deletes its contents, so on a few occasions when I employed this "fix" I had to then go find the IPs, passwords, etc. again. Additionally, there were a few times when I was actually unable to close the map application once I'd opened it. This didn't necessarily affect the gameplay, but it was irritating, as it helps me organize my evidence to only have relevant applications open at a given time.

I know that I've written a lot of words on the negatives of the game, but it's only because I'd love to see this title reach its potential, and/or see a Mainlining 2. If you enjoy these types of experiences (similar to Hacknet, Orwell, etc.), you'll have fun with Mainlining.

Mainlining is a nifty little adventure game with a hacking theme that, unlike other hacking games available on steam, eschews the nitty gritty of command-line interface wizardry in favor of telling a succint story well within its means.  That is to say, if you've avoided other hacking games because they emulate real-world operating systems all too closely, you can relax - Mainlining's CLI is quite simple and doesn't require any foreknowledge of how command-line operating systems work.

Instead of bringing the hardcore keyboard thunder, Mainlining opts for funtional aesthetics.  When you first start up the game, you'll be looking at a pixelated mock-up of a WinXP-like desktop.  Though typing away in the CLI is a big part of the game, you'll only ever need three or four commands, all of which are easy to remember.  The rest is as you would normally navigate a desktop OS these days - with a mouse.  Throughout the game, you will load applications onto your start bar, read files on your desktop notepad, and browse a well-realized fake web, all the while using information you find to remotely hack into other systems.  Throughout several cases, you will follow a bread-crumb trail that will eventually unravel to reveal a story.

That story being you work for MI7, a sister org to the famous MI5, only its main focus is online activity facilitating real-world crimes, and the backdrop of all this is a new act simply called the BLU Pill.  While it never gets into specifics, BLU Pill basically enables the gov't to break into systems legally in order to fight crime.  Naturally, this angers a few people and they organize themselves into a secret hacking group to counter MI7's efforts.  The game makes no hard stance on the politics of such a law, but throughout the game, you're never quite sure if you're the good guy or the bad guy.

In any case, this is all handled with beautiful pixel-style art from end-to-end, from presenting you nostalgic mock-ups of popular desktops (WinXP, iOS, etc) to a whole database full of pixel faces of the citizens of wherever you are.  In terms of aesthetics, Mainlining really reminded me of Digital A Love Story, and it unfolds in a very similar manner.  As you read chat logs and other random files you nab off unsuspecting systems, you'll learn about the inhabitants of this world and the characters found therein.  Moreover, there are live chat windows on your screen that dole out large portions of the story and all you ever have are names.  You're not told who's who, but it eventually all slots into place.

While I didn't encounter any glaring bugs, the game doesn't give you a lot of options to go off-script, nor does it make any effort throw any red herrings at you so unless you're really trying to find ways to break the game, you likely won't have a problem.  At all times, I was patienly waiting for the proverbial Other Shoe, but it never really came.  As each day/case passes, you'll be told what you need to find in order to proceed and any previously-learned knowledge usually doesn't work again, so going off the beaten path doesn't really present itself.  You either figure out what to do next or you don't.

That being said, I completed the game in about 2 hours or so and never even so much as wished for a hint.  All of the challenges in the game are easily met and good segments of the game are just waiting around for some things to happen.  I can't really describe more since that would spoil it, but for the most part, it plays a lot like the old standard of cutscene -> gameplay -> cutscene.

All in all, I found Mainlining to be an enjoyable experience and a perfect entry point into the genre since it really does a little of everything.  Outside of some proofreading mishaps, the game is solid.

TL;DR (good deal of gameplay from free demo):  Mainlining is a fun adventure game with a clever and unique twist where you hack computers, websites, and other devices to mine information on the different cases presented to you.  The game doesn't hold your hand, so the cases can present a fun little challenge beyond the first tutorial.  Highly recommended!  If you want to see a playthrough of the first (tutorial) case, check out this video (Demo version):

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kek4zO0OF_8

FULL REVIEW:  Mainlining, the point-and-click hacking adventure game, casts the player as an employee of MI7 in charge of investigating various cyber-crimes and tracking suspects through electronic means.  You are given tools (e.g., electronic trackers, a simplified command-line, web browser, etc) in order to collect information, put together clues, and ultimately arrest the right person.

There is a lot of unique gameplay in Mainlining since, unlike other adventure games, the puzzles and stories you try to untangle are pieced together from short emails, blog posts, and other electronic files.  The game does a good job of not holding your hand (e.g., by telling you which sites to hack, etc) but does provide sufficient in-context clues so that the task isn’t impossible and/or a guessing game.  It’s also a game that very much should be played with a pen and paper handy because you’ll need to track which websites/IP addresses you have collected, which you have hacked, which files you have or have not read or downloaded, and which suspects you wish to pursue.  Note that there IS a “notes” application (because the game looks like a computer desktop), but that fills up quickly.

Overall, the game is challenging, unique, and very entertaining (it’s got a good self-aware/internet-aware sense of humor) while still retaining the hallmarks of good adventure games: good story, good gameplay mechanics, and good pacing.  I would definitely recommend this game or, at the least, would suggest you check out the demo (which contains the first two cases from the full game—and save files apparently carry over).
